title: Does tempo equal offense success in the Big Ten?
text:
Code

Here I created a file set that filtered for just the Big Ten teams, filtering the teams in the conference. Then we took the nunmber of total plays divided by the amount of games that the teams played in.


Code
bigten24 <- logs24 |>
  filter(Conference == "Big Ten Conference")

bigten25 <- logs25 |>
  filter(Conference == "Big Ten Conference")




Code
avg_plays_24 <- bigten24 |>
  group_by(Team) |>
  summarize(avg_plays = mean(TotalPlays, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(season = "2024")

avg_plays_25 <- bigten25 |>
  group_by(Team) |>
  summarize(avg_plays = mean(TotalPlays, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(season = "2025")


Sometimes, team’s offenses run a lot of plays because they want to speed up the pace of the game. But other times, it’s because their defense is unable to get any stops. Ocassionaly, it’s both. That’s what happened with 2024 Maryland, who had one of the worst passing defenses in the Big Ten, allowing opponents to throw for over 300 yards per game in a majority of its Big Ten contests. The Terps’ offense was constantly on the field and trying to play catch up, which led to them running the most amunt of plays.


Code
ggplot(avg_plays_24, aes(x = reorder(Team, avg_plays), y = avg_plays)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1f77b4") +
  coord_flip() +
 labs(title = "Maryland football finished 4-8.", subtitle = "It still ran the most offensive plays in the Big Ten",
    x = "Team",
    y = "Average Offensive Plays"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









But this season, we’ve seen some drastic shifts in the conference. Ohio State, who has some of the most offensive firepower in the nation, runs the least amount of plays in the Big Ten. That’s most likely due to the Buckeyes’ blowing out several teams, but they also have had one of the nation’s best defenses, and this is a somewhat troubling sign for Ohio State’s future. One other takeaway: teams with strong and older quarterbacks tend to run more plays. Seven of the top eight teams have either old quarterbacks or a strong true freshman signal-caller in the case of Maryland and Malik Washington.


Code
ggplot(avg_plays_25, aes(x = reorder(Team, avg_plays), y = avg_plays)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#ff7f0e") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Ohio State's offense is dominant despite not running plays",
    x = "Team",
    y = "Average Offensive Plays"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

teams <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/NCAAWomensVolleyballData/main/data/ncaa_womens_volleyball_matchstats_2025.csv")

library(waffle)




Code
md <- teams |>
  filter(team == "Maryland") |>
  summarise(
    kills = sum(kills, na.rm = TRUE),
    blocks = sum(block_solos + block_assists, na.rm = TRUE),
    aces = sum(aces, na.rm = TRUE),
    opp_errors = sum(defensive_errors, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

  "Kills" = 525,
  "Blocks" = 216,
  "Aces" = 72,
  "Opponent Errors" = 257
) / 5




Code

  md,
  rows = 10,
  title = "Maryland's Offense",
  xlab = "1 square = 5 points",
  colors = c("black", "red", "gold", "gray80")
)











Code
neb <- teams |>
  filter(team == "Nebraska") |>
  summarise(
    kills = sum(kills, na.rm = TRUE),
    blocks = sum(block_solos + block_assists, na.rm = TRUE),
    aces = sum(aces, na.rm = TRUE),
    opp_errors = sum(defensive_errors, na.rm = TRUE)
  )




Code
neb <- c(
  "Kills" = 777,
  "Blocks" = 258,
  "Aces" = 60,
  "Opponent Errors" = 325
) / 5




Code
waffle(
  neb,
  rows = 10,
  title = "Nebraska's offense",
  xlab = "1 square = 5 points",
  colors = c("red", "tan", "black", "gray80")
)









Nebraska’s offense is one of the best in the country, compared to Maryland who’s struggled. The Huskers’ offense dominates the kill battle, scoring more than 50% of their points with kills at the net, along with blocks. They have built one of the more dominant front lines in the country, led by All-American Harper Murray, so this scoring distrubtion makes sense. Meanwhile, Maryland’s aces actually predicate alot of its scoring, compared to Nebraska. The Terps score a good portion of their points via aces, but they’re not forcing opponents to make errors, which is something Nebraska excels at with their pressure and strong shots at the net.

Code
suppressMessages(library(tidyverse))




Code
logs <- read_csv("footballlogs1525.csv")


Rows: 17133 Columns: 79
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (11): Location, Opponent, Result, OT, Bowl.x, TeamURL, Outcome, Bowl.y,...

date  (1): Date

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


Code
logs <- logs |> mutate(Season = case_when(
  month(Date) == 1 ~ year(Date) - 1,
  .default = year(Date)
))

season_games <- logs |>
  group_by(Season) |>
  summarise(games = n())

season_games_under_100_wins <- logs |>
  filter(Result == "W", RushYds < 100) |>
  group_by(Season) |>
  summarise(low_rush_wins = n()) 

combined_games <- season_games |> 
  inner_join(season_games_under_100_wins, join_by(Season)) |>
  mutate(low_pct_rush_wins = low_rush_wins/games * 100)




Code
big_ten_season_games <- logs |>
   filter(Conference == "Big Ten Conference") |>
  group_by(Season) |>
  summarise(big_ten_games = n())

b10_under_100_wins <- logs |>
  filter(Conference == "Big Ten Conference", Result == "W", RushYds < 100) |>
  group_by(Season) |>
  summarise(big_ten_low_rush_wins = n()) 

final_big_ten <- big_ten_season_games |> 
  inner_join(b10_under_100_wins, join_by(Season)) |>
  mutate(big_ten_low_pct_rush_wins = big_ten_low_rush_wins/big_ten_games * 100)




Code
ncaa_vs_big_ten <- combined_games |> 
  inner_join(final_big_ten, join_by(Season))


Run the ball and prosper. When people picture Big Ten football, box scores of sub-100 passing yard days, trench warefare between offensive and defensive lines and ground-and-pound offenses pop to mind.
Jim Harbaugh’s four tight end formations, Iowa’s commitment to avoiding an efficient passing game like the plauge and the great running backs who have come through the conference (Jonathan Taylor, Kenneth Walker and Blake Corum). It’s the brand of the Big Ten: we run the ball better than anyone.
But the numbers don’t suggest that, entirely. The Big Ten actually has a number of teams who can win games without rushing the ball effectively. Compared to the NCAA average, the conference has actually become a more pass-happy league over recent years. In 2022, Big Ten teams who rushed for less than 100 yards still 9% of the conference’s total games, compared to the NCAA average of just under 6%.


Code
ggplot(ncaa_vs_big_ten, aes(x = Season)) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = low_pct_rush_wins, color = "NCAA")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = big_ten_low_pct_rush_wins, color = "Big Ten")) +
  labs(
    title = "Low Rush Percentage Wins: NCAA vs Big Ten",
    x = "Season", 
    y = "Low Rush Win Percentage",
    color = "Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("NCAA" = "steelblue", "Big Ten" = "darkred")) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = ~ axisTicks(., log = FALSE))









Recent years have showed that the league has seen drastic shifts to becoming a more passing league. Teams like Ohio State, Maryland and others have changed the formula for how the league can win games.
But 2025 has been a shift back to normal. Despite the small sample size, the Big Ten has fallen back to NCAA avergae on teams winning games without rushing for more than 100 yards. So maybe, we’re back to the Big Ten styles that past generations grew up with.

I found that teams tyipcally pass the ball much more on third and medium than they do run the ball. In fact, more often there’s an incomplete pass than there is a run play. That’s because those third and six rush plays don’t average out to get the first down, it’s on average a yard short of the mark. That’s a encouraging sign for teams who are looking to run the ball on third and six and then go for it on fourth down, as the average would lend to them getting just one yard short of the first down.

But how do they stack up compared to the Big Ten? Well, historically high. The number of snaps defensive freshman have played for the Terps this season is signficantly higher than the rest of the conference. In fact, the next closest team – Michian – has played freshman almost a third of the time compared to Maryland. The youngest team is going through struggles and while some of this can be placed on the Terps youthness, these are also experienced players at this point. Locksley said the same thing at his recent presser, saying the freshman have become experienced at this point. At this point, Maryland has no excuses.
